about: A fast web browser that runs without a screen, made for bots and AI agents that read websites.

prs.title: The :default selector works
prs.broken: The :default selector never matched, so forms' default buttons and options could not be found.
prs.changed: It now finds the default button, checked boxes and selected options.
prs.matters: Form automation finds the same elements as in Chrome.

prs.title: The :scope selector works on a page
prs.broken: Searching a page with :scope found nothing at all.
prs.changed: It now matches the top of the page, as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Scripts that use :scope work in Lightpanda.

prs.title: Empty attribute filters match nothing
prs.broken: Searching for elements whose attribute starts, ends or contains an empty value matched every such element.
prs.changed: These searches now match nothing, as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Scripts and scrapers get the same results as in a real browser.

prs.title: Playwright mouse drags and Puppeteer drag and drop now work
prs.broken: Playwright asks the browser to watch for drags during every mouse move with the button held. Lightpanda did not know that request, so pressing and moving the mouse, or dragging one element onto another, failed.
prs.changed: Lightpanda now answers that request, and can play drag and drop events sent from outside the page in the same order Chrome fires them, carrying the dragged text or links.
prs.matters: Scripts that drag sliders, reorder lists or drop files and links onto a page can run in Lightpanda.

prs.title: Required and optional field rules match only real form fields
prs.broken: The page rules that pick out required and optional fields matched almost anything. A small form page had 47 optional elements instead of 9, and hidden inputs counted as required.
prs.changed: Only the form fields that can be required now match, using the same list Chrome uses: text inputs and similar, selects, text areas, and buttons for optional.
prs.matters: Scripts that look for empty required fields, or styles that mark them, get the same answer as in Chrome.

prs.title: Mouse enter and leave handlers set on an element now run
prs.broken: Pages can attach a hover handler straight to an element, the window or the document. Lightpanda did not know the mouse enter and leave versions, so menus and tooltips built that way never reacted.
prs.changed: Elements, the document and the window now accept both handlers, and they run when the mouse moves onto or off an element, as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Scripts that hover over menus or tooltips see the same page a real browser shows.

prs.title: Playwright can click inside shadow DOM
prs.broken: Shadow roots were missing the lookup that finds which element sits at a point on the page. Playwright uses it before every click, so clicking any element inside a shadow root failed with an error.
prs.changed: Shadow roots now have both lookups and return the same answers as Chrome, including for nested shadow roots.
prs.matters: Pages built with web components can be driven by Playwright in Lightpanda.

prs.title: Jumping to a spot on the same page now updates the address
prs.broken: When a page used the newer navigation tool to jump to a spot on the same page, the address did not change, history saved a half-written address, and styles for that spot did not apply. Chrome does all three.
prs.changed: Every jump within the same page now updates the address, saves the full address in history, and restyles the targeted spot, like Chrome.
prs.matters: Pages and scripts that move around a single page see the same address in Lightpanda as in Chrome.

prs.title: Number fields now flag values that are off their step
prs.broken: A number field with a step, like 0.01 for cents, never reported a value such as 1.005 as invalid. Form checks that rely on it let bad values through.
prs.changed: I made the browser check whether the value lands on a step, with room for rounding so large values like 1234567.89 still count as valid, and made the step up and step down buttons use the same check.
prs.matters: Forms with number fields validate the same way they do in Chrome.

prs.title: Scripts can now replace text inside form fields
prs.broken: Text boxes were missing a standard way to swap out part of their text. Editors, input masks and helpers that insert text at the cursor crashed on pages run in Lightpanda.
prs.changed: Text boxes and text areas now have it, following the web standard, including where the selection ends up afterwards.
prs.matters: Pages with rich text boxes and formatted inputs work for bots the same as in Chrome.

prs.title: Pages can now pick the second item of a kind in a list
prs.broken: Web pages can find, say, the second item in a list that has a given style. Lightpanda did not understand that form of the rule, threw an error, and the page script stopped.
prs.changed: The rule now works for counting from the start and from the end, and matches what Chrome finds.
prs.matters: Sites that use it to find or style elements keep running instead of breaking halfway.

prs.title: Cookies are now sent in the order browsers send them
prs.broken: The browser listed cookies in the order they were set. Real browsers put longer paths first, then older cookies. When two cookies share a name, many servers keep only the first one, so they could read the wrong value.
prs.changed: Cookies are now sorted by path length and then by age, both when a page reads them and when a request sends them.
prs.matters: Sites that rely on cookie order behave the same as in a normal browser.

prs.title: Markdown pages come through as plain markdown
prs.broken: A page served as markdown was wrapped in a code block when converted, and a code block inside the file could end it early. There was also no way to use the markdown version a page offers as an alternate.
prs.changed: Markdown files are now written out as they are. A new opt-in setting follows a page's markdown alternate when it has one, and the output says which source was used.
prs.matters: AI agents get clean markdown from sites that publish it.

prs.title: Typing in a box now tells the page the value changed
prs.broken: Pages often wait for a 'changed' signal before they check, save or filter what was typed. Chrome sends it when you leave the box or press Enter. This browser never sent it, so those pages never saw the typed text.
prs.changed: The browser now remembers the value from before the typing and sends the signal on leaving the box or pressing Enter, if the value is different, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Forms that check or save what you type now work for bots too.

prs.title: Filter and sort forms now send the new choice
prs.broken: When a form like 'sort by' was sent from a page whose address already held choices, the browser added the new choice instead of replacing the old one. With a '#' in the address, the form was never sent.
prs.changed: The browser now swaps the old choices for the form's and keeps the '#' part at the end, as the web standard says and Chrome does.
prs.matters: Bots that filter, sort or search through forms land on the page they asked for.

prs.title: A '?' after the '#' in a link no longer changes the address
prs.broken: Many web apps put a '?' after the '#' in their links. The browser read it as part of the real address, so edited links went somewhere else and servers were told text meant to stay in the browser.
prs.changed: The browser now only looks for the '?' before the '#', like Chrome does.
prs.matters: Links in these apps go where they should, and the private part of the address stays private.

prs.title: Searches for forms and links now ignore letter case, like Chrome
prs.broken: Pages often write things like method="POST". Searching the page for forms with method=post found nothing, though Chrome finds them, so bots missed forms and links.
prs.changed: For the attributes where the web standard says case doesn't matter, the search now ignores it.
prs.matters: Bots and test tools find the same parts of a page that Chrome does.

prs.title: Saved logins now survive being restored
prs.broken: Programs that save a logged-in session and load it later got back a logged-out one. The browser misread the login cookies' 'no end date' mark as 'expired' and dropped them.
prs.changed: The browser now keeps those cookies until the session ends, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Bots can log in once and reuse that login, instead of ending up signed out.

prs.title: Dropdown choices now send clean text
prs.broken: Dropdown choices kept the extra spaces and line breaks from the page's source code. Forms sent the server garbled values, and picking a choice by name found nothing.
prs.changed: The browser now trims and squeezes that extra space, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Servers get the same form answers they would get from Chrome.

prs.title: Ctrl+A now selects all the text in a box
prs.broken: Pressing Ctrl+A in a text box did nothing. Programs that clear a field by selecting all and typing over it ended up with the old text plus the new.
prs.changed: The browser now selects everything in the box on Ctrl+A, like Chrome on Linux.
prs.matters: A common way scripts clear and refill form fields now works.

prs.title: A missing table feature no longer breaks page searches
prs.broken: Pages couldn't ask a table for its rows. Playwright, a popular tool for driving browsers, needs that, so on some pages with tables every search for a heading or button crashed.
prs.changed: I added the list of rows, in the order the web standard sets out.
prs.matters: Playwright scripts that find links, buttons and headings by what they are now work on those pages.

prs.title: Error messages from a page now reach the program
prs.broken: When code run on a page failed, the program controlling the browser got an empty error message, or just 'undefined', instead of the real one Chrome gives.
prs.changed: The browser now labels page objects correctly, so real errors keep their message.
prs.matters: Developers see what actually went wrong instead of a blank error.

prs.title: Deleting a cookie now actually deletes it
prs.broken: Sites often delete a cookie (a small note a site stores in the browser) by giving it a 1970 expiry date ending in 'UTC'. The browser misread that, so the cookie stayed.
prs.changed: I taught the browser to read dates ending in 'UTC', so those cookies are removed as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Log-out and cookie-consent code that clears cookies this way now works.

prs.title: The browser's own tests stop hiding failures
prs.broken: In the project's test suite, a test that crashed after its first check passed still counted as passed. One test had been quietly skipping its later checks this way.
prs.changed: I made a crash anywhere in a test count as a failure, and fixed the test it had been hiding.
prs.matters: Behind-the-scenes work, but future bugs can't slip past tests that only look like they passed.

prs.title: Searches inside news feeds and drawings now find items
prs.broken: Programs looking up parts of a page by name came up empty in two cases: inside RSS news feeds, and for some drawing elements with capital letters in their names.
prs.changed: I made the browser match those names properly; one small upper/lowercase difference from Chrome is left.
prs.matters: Scripts that read news feeds or graphics on a page now find what is there.

prs.title: Custom page elements are now told apart by name
prs.broken: Sites can invent their own element types, like a 'card'. Asked for 'the second card', the browser lumped all invented types together and picked the wrong one, or none.
prs.changed: The browser now treats each invented element name as its own type, as Chrome does.
prs.matters: Scripts that pick the first, second or last of a kind of item now get the right one.

prs.title: The page clock now reports the real date
prs.broken: A page asking when it was opened got the time since the computer started, not the real date and time, so its date math was off by decades.
prs.changed: The browser now records the real clock time when a page opens and reports that.
prs.matters: Page scripts that log or measure time get correct timestamps.

prs.title: A space before a closing bracket is no longer an error
prs.broken: Page lookups like 'every odd item in a list' failed with an error if there was a space before the closing bracket, even though the rules allow it.
prs.changed: The browser now skips spaces there, as the styling rules allow.
prs.matters: Small fix. Valid page code written with extra spaces no longer stops with an error.

prs.title: Clearing text no longer writes the word 'null'
prs.broken: When a page cleared an element's text by setting it to 'nothing' (null), the browser showed the word 'null' instead of empty text.
prs.changed: The browser now treats 'nothing' as empty text, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Small fix, but pages no longer show a stray 'null' where text should be blank.

prs.title: Timers with a negative delay now go off
prs.broken: A page timer set with a negative or very large delay was misread as about 49 days, so it never went off. Chrome runs it right away.
prs.changed: The browser now treats such delays as zero, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Page code that schedules work this way now runs instead of silently waiting.

prs.title: The browser now knows which fields can be typed in
prs.broken: Asked which form fields can be typed into, the browser also counted checkboxes and disabled boxes, and said no field was read-only.
prs.changed: I made it follow the web standard's rules for what counts as editable.
prs.matters: Scripts and page styles that treat locked fields differently now see the same fields Chrome does.

prs.title: Saving a page's code no longer drops template parts
prs.broken: Pages can hold hidden 'template' blocks used to build content later. When the browser turned a page back into code, those blocks came out empty.
prs.changed: The browser now writes out what is inside templates, as the web standard says.
prs.matters: Saved copies of pages, including the browser's own page-dump command, keep all their content.

prs.title: Backspace, Tab and the arrow keys work now
prs.broken: When a program typed on a page, keys that don't type a letter (Backspace, Delete, arrows, Escape) were silently ignored. Pressing Backspace in a text box deleted nothing.
prs.changed: The browser now handles those key presses the same way Chrome does.
prs.matters: Scripts that fill in forms behave the same here as in a normal browser.

prs.title: Form fields are checked as valid or invalid the way browsers do
prs.broken: Web pages can style or find form fields that are filled in wrong. Lightpanda only noticed empty required fields, so a bad email address or a number below the limit counted as valid.
prs.changed: I made it use every rule a field has, like format, pattern, limits and custom messages, and leave out disabled fields.
prs.matters: Scripts and tests that look for invalid fields get the same answer as in Chrome.

prs.title: Sliders and color pickers start with their default value
prs.broken: A slider or color picker on a web form with no starting value was empty instead of its default, the middle of the range or black. Forms sent an empty field.
prs.changed: I made these fields start at their default, and go back to it when a form is reset.
prs.matters: Forms filled in by Lightpanda send the same values a regular browser would.

prs.title: Pages can ask for the window size and position
prs.broken: Lightpanda had no outer window size or screen position. Pages that use them, like the common code that centers a popup, broke with an error or got nonsense numbers.
prs.changed: I added them. The outer size matches the page size, since there is no window frame, and the position is the top left corner.
prs.matters: Pages that place popups or check the window size work the same as in a regular browser.

prs.title: Dropdown options know their position
prs.broken: In Lightpanda, asking a dropdown option for its position in the list gave nothing, while real browsers give a number.
prs.changed: I added the position, counted the same way browsers count it, including options inside groups.
prs.matters: Scripts that read which option is which work the same in Lightpanda as in Chrome.

prs.title: A form's list of fields includes every kind of field
prs.broken: When a script asked a form for its fields, Lightpanda left out fieldsets, outputs and embedded objects, so counts and positions differed from real browsers.
prs.changed: I made the list include those three kinds too, in page order, the way the HTML standard and Chrome do.
prs.matters: Scripts that walk a form by position or by name get the same fields in Lightpanda as in Chrome.

prs.title: Non-breaking spaces in attribute values now print as in Chrome
prs.broken: When a page was turned back into HTML, a non-breaking space in text was written safely, but in an attribute value it was written raw. Chrome writes it safely in both places.
prs.changed: Attribute values now get the same treatment as text, so the output matches Chrome.
prs.matters: Saved or compared page markup is the same as what Chrome produces.

prs.title: Text boxes now report their length and fix line breaks
prs.broken: A multi-line text box had no length value, and it kept Windows-style line breaks in what it returned. Chrome reports a length and turns every line break into a plain one.
prs.changed: The browser now reports the length the way Chrome does and cleans up line breaks when a value is set.
prs.matters: Scripts that read text boxes get the same answers as in Chrome.

prs.title: Cursor positions in text boxes now count characters like Chrome does
prs.broken: Where the cursor or selection sat in a text box was counted in raw bytes. Accents and emoji take several bytes, so scripts saw wrong positions and could place the cursor inside a character.
prs.changed: Positions are now counted the way web pages count them, and a position inside a character moves to its start.
prs.matters: Scripts that work with selections get correct results for accents and emoji.

prs.title: Text decoding now keeps the encoding a page asked for
prs.broken: When text started with certain marker bytes, the browser quietly switched to a different text encoding than the one the page asked for. Chrome only drops a marker that matches the chosen encoding.
prs.changed: The browser now sticks to the requested encoding and only removes a matching marker, the way Chrome does.
prs.matters: Pages that decode bytes into text get the same result as in Chrome, instead of garbled or wrongly shortened text.

prs.title: Changing part of a link's address keeps the rest of it
prs.broken: Setting one part of a link's address, like its port, dropped the user name and password, and bad values such as a port with letters were kept. Chrome keeps the rest and ignores bad values.
prs.changed: Each change now goes through the same address parser the browser already uses elsewhere, so bad values leave the link unchanged.
prs.matters: Pages that edit links by parts get the same addresses they would in Chrome.

prs.title: An empty password field no longer looks filled
prs.broken: Every password field showed a masked value in the accessibility and page dumps, so tools could not tell an empty field from a filled one.
prs.changed: An empty password field now shows no value. A filled one is still masked, so the typed password never appears.
prs.matters: Automation and agents can see which login fields still need filling.

prs.title: Page listeners run in the page's own context
prs.broken: When a tool like Playwright focused a field or picked a select option, the page's own event listeners ran in the tool's context and saw the wrong objects.
prs.changed: Each listener now runs in the context it was created in, whoever caused the event.
prs.matters: React focus and change handlers now fire when Playwright drives the page, as in Chrome.

prs.title: Clearing a style with null shows the element again
prs.broken: Pages often hide an element and later clear the style by setting it to null. The browser stored the word "null" instead, so the element stayed broken.
prs.changed: Setting a style property to null now clears it, as the web standard and Chrome do.
prs.matters: Menus, popups and other elements that pages show this way appear when they should.

prs.title: Page scripts set by test tools now run where pages can see them
prs.broken: When a test tool loaded HTML into Lightpanda, the page's own scripts ran in a hidden side area, so their variables and functions were missing.
prs.changed: Scripts on the page now always run in the page itself, as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Automated tests that load page content directly behave the same in Lightpanda as in Chrome.

prs.title: Email fields are checked the way Chrome checks them
prs.broken: Email form fields rejected good addresses like a@localhost and accepted broken ones like a@b..c. Fields that allow several addresses were not handled at all.
prs.changed: Addresses are now checked by the web standard's rules, and fields with several addresses are split and checked one by one.
prs.matters: Forms that check email input behave the same in Lightpanda as in Chrome.

prs.title: Custom data attributes follow the same rules as in Chrome
prs.broken: The way pages store custom data on elements accepted names the standard forbids, and turned a leading capital letter into a different name than Chrome does.
prs.changed: Bad names are now rejected with the same errors Chrome gives, and every capital letter is mapped the standard way.
prs.matters: Pages and scripts that store data on elements get the same results as in Chrome.

prs.title: Web requests that cannot have a body now refuse one
prs.broken: A page could send a GET or HEAD request with a body. Real browsers refuse that, so pages that test for it behaved differently in Lightpanda.
prs.changed: Such a request now fails with the same error a browser gives.
prs.matters: Sites and scripts see the same rules they see in Chrome, so automated runs match real use.

prs.title: Text hidden in a closed details box stays out of page text
prs.broken: Reading the visible text of a page included loose text inside a closed details box, which a real browser hides.
prs.changed: That text is now left out until the box is opened, as in Chrome.
prs.matters: Scripts and agents reading the page see what a person would see.
